title: Securing FastAPI: CORS and Essential Headers
description: Configure CORS and essential security headers in a FastAPI application.
content:
Hello and welcome back! In our last lesson, we built a sophisticated API endpoint with dynamic filtering, sorting, and pagination. Our backend is now highly functional, but if we tried to connect our React frontend to it, we'd run into a wall. Similarly, if we deployed it, it would be missing some standard protections that modern web applications are expected to have. This lesson directly addresses those gaps. We'll focus on **configuring Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) and essential security headers in your FastAPI application**. These are not optional extras; they are fundamental requirements for building secure, browser-compatible full-stack applications that you'd be expected to understand in any MNC environment. By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: * Explain the browser's Same-Origin Policy and why CORS is necessary. * Implement and configure `CORSMiddleware` in FastAPI to allow your frontend to communicate with your backend. * Create a custom middleware to add crucial HTTP security headers to every response, protecting your application from common web vulnerabilities. Let's secure our API. ### 1. The "Why": Same-Origin Policy and CORS Before we write any code, it's critical to understand the problem we're solving. Web browsers enforce a security mechanism called the **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)**. This policy dictates that a web page can only freely access resources (like making API calls) from the **same origin** from which the page itself was loaded. An "origin" is defined by the combination of **protocol** (e.g., `http`), **domain** (e.g., `localhost`), and **port** (e.g., `:3000`). Here’s why this is a problem for us: * Your React development server runs at `http://localhost:5173` (or `:3000`). * Your FastAPI backend server runs at `http://localhost:8000`. Even though they're both on `localhost`, the different ports mean they are **different origins**. When your React app tries to fetch data from `http://localhost:8000/todos`, the browser will block the request and show an error in the console, citing a violation of the SOP. **Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)** is the mechanism that fixes this. It's a system of HTTP headers that a server can send to tell the browser that it's okay to allow a web page from a different origin to access its resources. For many API requests (e.g., a `POST` with a JSON body, or any request with an `Authorization` header), the browser first sends a special "preflight" request using the `OPTIONS` HTTP method. The server must respond to this preflight request with the correct CORS headers, essentially giving permission, before the browser will send the actual `GET` or `POST` request. ### 2. Implementing CORS in FastAPI FastAPI provides a simple and effective way to manage CORS through its built-in `CORSMiddleware`. This middleware automatically intercepts incoming requests, handles preflight `OPTIONS` requests, and adds the correct CORS headers to your responses. To begin, please read about configuring CORS in the following resources. They highlight best practices for both development and production. ```grasp { "type": "reading", "title": "FastAPI production deployment best practices", "id": "[LINK](https://render.com/articles/fastapi-production-deployment-best-practices)", "url": "https://render.com/articles/fastapi-production-deployment-best-practices", "relevant_section_indices": [ 0, 1 ], "par_intro": "This article from Render's blog explains the core concepts of configuring CORS in a production-oriented way.", "par_directions": "Please read the section 'CORS configuration' and review the accompanying code block. Focus on the explanation of why using a wildcard `\"*\"` is discouraged in production.", "estimated_time": "5 minutes" } ``` ```grasp { "type": "reading", "title": "How to Secure FastAPI Applications Against OWASP Top 10", "id": "[LINK](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2025-01-06-fastapi-owasp-security/view)", "url": "https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2025-01-06-fastapi-owasp-security/view", "relevant_section_indices": [ 1 ], "par_intro": "This second article from OneUptime reinforces the same concepts and introduces the excellent practice of loading allowed origins from environment variables, which is a key pattern for managing different deployment environments.", "par_directions": "Read the section 'CORS Configuration' and its code example. Pay close attention to how it retrieves the list of allowed origins from `os.getenv`.", "estimated_time": "5 minutes" } ``` Based on what you've read, let's put it into practice. You add the `CORSMiddleware` to your main application instance. Here is a robust configuration that combines these best practices: ```python from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware import os app = FastAPI() # In a real application, you'd pull this from a config file or environment variables # For example, using a comma-separated string in an env var: # ALLOWED_ORIGINS="http://localhost:5173,https://my-prod-app.com" # We'll simulate that here: allowed_origins_str = os.getenv("ALLOWED_ORIGINS", "http://localhost:5173") allowed_origins = allowed_origins_str.split(",") # Add the CORS middleware to the application app.add_middleware( CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=allowed_origins, # List of origins that are allowed to make cross-origin requests allow_credentials=True, # Allow cookies and authorization headers allow_methods=["*"], # Allow all standard methods (GET, POST, etc.) allow_headers=["*"], # Allow all headers ) # ... your API routers and endpoints ``` Let's break down the key parameters: * `allow_origins`: This is the most critical part. It's a list of the specific frontend origins that are allowed to access your API. In production, this should be your frontend's domain (e.g., `https://www.your-app.com`). Using a wildcard `"*"` is insecure because it allows *any* site to make requests, and browsers will disallow sending credentials (like cookies or auth tokens) to a wildcard origin. * `allow_credentials`: Set this to `True` to allow your frontend to include cookies or `Authorization` headers in its requests, which is essential for authentication. * `allow_methods`: Specifies which HTTP methods are allowed. `["*"]` is often fine for convenience. * `allow_headers`: Specifies which HTTP request headers are allowed. `["*"]` is also a common convenience here, but you could lock it down to `["Content-Type", "Authorization"]` for more security.
Test your understanding! Your company is setting up a new project. * The frontend team develops on `http://localhost:5173`. * A QA team needs to test the API from a staging frontend deployed at `https://staging.my-app.com`. * The final production frontend will live at `https://www.my-app.com`. You are configuring the API for the **staging environment**. Which list of origins should you use for `allow_origins`?
Show answer The correct configuration for the staging environment would be: `allow_origins=["http://localhost:5173", "https://staging.my-app.com"]` This allows both the local developers and the QA team on the staging domain to access the API. The production domain (`https://www.my-app.com`) should *not* be included here; it belongs in the production configuration. This separation of environments is a critical security practice.
### 3. Adding Essential Security Headers CORS allows your frontend to talk to your backend. Security headers, on the other hand, are instructions your backend sends to the browser to tell it to enable built-in security features. This provides "defense in depth" against common attacks like Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and clickjacking. The standard way to implement this in a FastAPI (or any Starlette-based) application is with a custom middleware. A middleware is a function that processes every request before it hits your endpoint and every response before it's sent to the client. The following resource provides an excellent, comprehensive example of a security headers middleware. ```grasp { "type": "reading", "title": "How to Secure FastAPI Applications Against OWASP Top 10", "id": "[LINK](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2025-01-06-fastapi-owasp-security/view)", "url": "https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2025-01-06-fastapi-owasp-security/view", "relevant_section_indices": [ 0 ], "par_intro": "Let's review a detailed implementation of a middleware that adds a suite of modern security headers to every response.", "par_directions": "Read the section 'Secure Headers Middleware'. Focus on the `SecurityHeadersMiddleware` class and the purpose of each header it adds. You don't need to memorize the exact syntax for each one, but understand what threat they help mitigate.", "estimated_time": "10 minutes" } ``` Let's implement this middleware in our application. You would create a new file, perhaps `app/middleware/security.py`, and place the class there. ```python # In app/middleware/security.py from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware from starlette.requests import Request class SecurityHeadersMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware): async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next): response = await call_next(request) # Instructs browsers to prefer HTTPS response.headers["Strict-Transport-Security"] = "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" # Prevents browsers from trying to guess the content type response.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff" # Prevents the page from being rendered in an
